title: FlashDecoding Under the Hood: Parallelizing KV-Cache Attention Along Sequence Length to Solve the Autoregressive Decoding Bottleneck
summary: While FlashAttention revolutionized large language model training and prompt prefill by computing exact attention in fast GPU on-chip SRAM, it falters during autoregressive generation at long context lengths. During the decoding phase, a model evaluates only a single query token (Q length = 1) against thousands or millions of cached Key and Value tokens. Because standard FlashAttention parallelizes work exclusively across batch size and query heads, small batch queries leave up to 80% of GPU Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) completely idle, severely throttling token generation speeds. FlashDecoding solves this architectural mismatch by parallelizing attention computation directly along the KV sequence length dimension. By splitting the KV cache into independent chunks, computing partial softmax reductions concurrently across all SMs, and synchronizing results with a tree reduction, FlashDecoding achieves up to 8x faster generation at long context lengths without changing model weights.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Single Inspector with a Warehouse vs. The Swarm of Section Inspectors
analogy:
Imagine a mega-warehouse containing 100,000 document files, and a company must check one new incoming invoice against every archived file to find relevant correlations.

Under Standard FlashAttention During Decoding (The Single Inspector), the company has 100 skilled inspectors (GPU Streaming Multiprocessors) standing ready in the lobby. But company policy dictates: 'Only one inspector per client account!' Because only one invoice is being processed (Batch size = 1), 1 inspector is assigned to read all 100,000 files one by one, while the other 99 inspectors stand around playing on their phones. Inspection takes minutes because 99% of available human compute is wasted.

Under FlashDecoding (The Swarm of Section Inspectors), the manager splits the warehouse into 100 equal aisles of 1,000 files each and sends all 100 inspectors into the aisles simultaneously. Each inspector computes an aisle-level partial correlation score in parallel. In the final five seconds, all 100 inspectors bring their summary scores to a supervisor who runs a quick mathematical consolidation (Log-Sum-Exp tree reduction). The entire warehouse check completes in fractions of a second, with 100% workforce utilization.

sections.heading: 1. Prefill vs. Generation: Why FlashAttention Fails During Single-Token Decoding
sections.content:
FlashAttention achieved dramatic speedups by tiling inputs to fit within fast GPU on-chip SRAM, avoiding slow round-trips to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). During the prompt prefill phase, queries and keys both span thousands of tokens ($S_Q = S_K$). The GPU easily parallelizes across batch size $B$, query heads $H$, and sequence length blocks, spawning thousands of concurrent thread blocks that fully occupy all 108–132 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) on NVIDIA A100 or H100 GPUs.

• The Autoregressive Under-Occupancy Trap: During token generation (decoding), the model computes attention for only a single new token at a time: $S_Q = 1$. Standard FlashAttention parallelizes solely across the $B \times H$ dimension. If an application serves a low-latency single user query ($B = 1$) on a model with 32 attention heads ($H = 32$), exactly 32 thread blocks are scheduled.
• Hardware Waste on Modern GPUs: An NVIDIA H100 GPU features 132 SMs. Scheduling only 32 thread blocks leaves 100 SMs (over 75% of the GPU) completely unallocated! Meanwhile, those 32 active thread blocks struggle to read megabytes of KV cache over the memory bus, dragging generation speeds down to an agonizing crawl.

sections.heading: 2. Sequence-Dimension Parallelization: Slicing the KV Cache Across SMs
sections.content:
FlashDecoding overcomes this hardware under-utilization by adding a new axis of parallelism: the Key and Value sequence dimension ($S_{KV}$):

• Chunked Sequence Tiling: Instead of forcing one thread block to traverse the entire context window for an attention head, FlashDecoding divides the historical KV cache into discrete sequence chunks of size $C$ (typically 256 or 512 tokens). For a sequence length of 32,768 tokens, $32,768 / 256 = 128$ independent chunks are created per head.
• Massive Thread Block Creation: With 32 attention heads and 128 chunks per head, FlashDecoding generates $32 \times 128 = 4,096$ concurrent thread blocks. Every single SM on the GPU is flooded with work. Multiple thread blocks execute simultaneously on each SM, masking memory fetch latencies and maximizing read throughput across the GPU's memory controllers.
• Kernel Fusion in SRAM: Each thread block executes the standard FlashAttention inner loop over its assigned chunk: loading the single query token into SRAM, streaming the 256 KV tokens, and calculating partial attention outputs entirely in registers and shared memory.

sections.heading: 3. Numerical Stability and The Log-Sum-Exp Reduction Tree
sections.content:
Because the softmax function $\text{softmax}(x)_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum e^{x_j}}$ is non-linear and requires the global maximum across all sequence tokens, combining results from independent chunks requires exact mathematical reduction:

• Tracking Partial Statistics: Each sequence chunk $k$ computes and outputs three values: the partial attention output vector $O^{(k)}$, the local maximum value $m^{(k)} = \max(x^{(k)})$, and the local accumulator $l^{(k)} = \sum e^{x^{(k)} - m^{(k)}}$. These small statistics are written to a lightweight intermediate staging buffer in global memory.
• The Rescaling Tree Reduction: Once all sequence chunks finish, a secondary, highly efficient reduction kernel is launched. It merges chunk pairs using the safe online softmax update formulas: $m = \max(m_1, m_2)$, and updates normalizers via $l = l_1 e^{m_1 - m} + l_2 e^{m_2 - m}$. The final output is rescaled as $O = O_1 \frac{l_1 e^{m_1 - m}}{l} + O_2 \frac{l_2 e^{m_2 - m}}{l}$.
• Negligible Synchronization Overhead: Because the reduction operates only on the aggregated chunk statistics (128 vectors per head) rather than individual tokens, the reduction phase consumes less than 1% of the total kernel execution time, delivering up to 8x end-to-end decoding speedups.

takeaway: Autoregressive LLM generation with long contexts is fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound and under-utilizes GPU cores due to single-token queries. FlashDecoding restores maximum GPU occupancy by partitioning the Key-Value sequence length across independent Streaming Multiprocessors, combining partial attention outputs via a lightweight log-sum-exp reduction tree to deliver up to 8x lower decoding latency.
